text:
“Do speak more quietly,” she said to him with a frightened look. Julien was trying to recall the phrases from an odd volume of the _New Heloise_ that he had found at Vergy. His memory served him well; for ten minutes he had been reciting the _New Heloise_ to a delighted Mademoiselle Amanda, and he was happy in his boldness, when suddenly the beautiful woman from Franche-Comté assumed an icy air. One of her lovers had appeared at the door of the café.

He approached the counter, whistling and swaggering his shoulders; he looked at Julien. At once, Julien’s imagination, always running to extremes, was filled with nothing but thoughts of a duel. He turned very pale, pushed his cup away, put on a confident expression, and looked at his rival very attentively. As this rival lowered his head while familiarly pouring himself a glass of brandy at the counter, Amanda ordered Julien with a glance to lower his eyes. He obeyed and, for two minutes, remained motionless in his place, pale, resolute, and thinking only of what was about to happen; he was truly admirable at that moment. The rival had been surprised by Julien’s eyes; having swallowed his glass of brandy in one gulp, he said a word to Amanda, put both hands into the side pockets of his heavy overcoat, and approached a billiard table, puffing and looking at Julien. Julien rose, carried away by anger; but he did not know how to go about being insolent. He put down his little bundle and, with the most swaggering air he could manage, walked toward the billiard table.

In vain prudence told him: But with a duel as soon as you arrive in Besançon, your ecclesiastical career is ruined.

What does it matter? It shall not be said that I let an insolent fellow escape me.

Amanda saw his courage; it formed a pretty contrast with the ingenuousness of his manners; in an instant, she preferred him to the tall young man in the overcoat. She rose and, while pretending to be following someone passing in the street with her eyes, quickly came and placed herself between him and the billiard table:

“Take care not to look askance at that gentleman; he is my brother-in-law.”

“What do I care? He looked at me.”

“Do you want to make me unhappy? Of course he looked at you; perhaps he is even going to come and speak to you. I told him that you are a relative of my mother’s and that you have just arrived from Genlis. He is from Franche-Comté and has never gone beyond Dole on the road to Burgundy; so say whatever you like, and do not be afraid.”

Julien was still hesitating; she added very quickly, her imagination as a woman behind a counter supplying her with lies in abundance:

“Of course he looked at you, but that was when he was asking me who you were; he is a man who is boorish with everyone; he did not mean to insult you.”

Julien’s eye followed the supposed brother-in-law; he saw him buy a number in the pool being played at the farther of the two billiard tables. Julien heard his loud voice cry in a threatening tone, “I’ll take the play.” He passed quickly behind Mademoiselle Amanda and took a step toward the billiard table. Amanda seized him by the arm:

“Come and pay me first,” she said to him.

That is fair, thought Julien; she is afraid I shall leave without paying.

Amanda was as agitated as he was and very red; she gave him his change as slowly as she could, all the while repeating to him in a low voice:

“Leave the café this instant, or I shall no longer love you; and yet I love you dearly.”

Julien did leave, but slowly. Is it not my duty, he kept asking himself, to go and stare at that coarse fellow in my turn, puffing as I do so? This uncertainty kept him for an hour on the boulevard in front of the café; he watched to see whether his man would come out. He did not appear, and Julien went away.

He had been in Besançon for only a few hours, and already he had acquired a remorse. The old surgeon-major had once given him, despite his gout, a few fencing lessons; that was all the skill Julien could find to put at the service of his anger. But this difficulty would have been nothing if he had known how to become angry otherwise than by administering a slap in the face; and if it came to fisticuffs, his rival, an enormous man, would have beaten him and then left him there.

For a poor devil like me, Julien said to himself, without protectors and without money, there will not be much difference between a seminary and a prison; I must leave my civilian clothes at some inn, where I shall put my black coat back on. If I ever manage to get out of the seminary for a few hours, I can quite easily put on my civilian clothes and see Mademoiselle Amanda again. This reasoning was excellent; but as Julien passed all the inns, he did not dare enter any of them.

At last, as he passed the Hôtel des Ambassadeurs again, his anxious eyes met those of a stout woman, still fairly young, ruddy, with a happy and cheerful air. He approached her and told her his story.

“Certainly, my pretty little abbé,” the landlady of the Ambassadeurs said to him, “I shall keep your civilian clothes for you and even have them dusted often. At this time of year, it is not wise to leave a woolen coat untouched.” She took a key and herself led him to a room, recommending that he write down a list of what he was leaving.

“Good Lord! How handsome you look like that, Monsieur l’Abbé Sorel,” the stout woman said to him when he came down to the kitchen. “I am going to have a good dinner served to you, and,” she added in a low voice, “it will cost you only twenty sous instead of the fifty everyone else pays; for you must take care of your little nest egg.”

“I have ten louis,” Julien replied with a certain pride.

“Oh, good Lord!” the kind landlady answered in alarm. “Do not speak so loudly; there are many bad characters in Besançon. They will steal that from you in no time. Above all, never go into the cafés; they are full of bad characters.”

“Really!” said Julien, to whom this remark gave food for thought.

“Never go anywhere but here; I shall have coffee made for you. Remember that you will always find a friend here and a good dinner for twenty sous; that is plain speaking, I hope. Go and sit down at the table; I shall serve you myself.”

“I could not eat,” Julien told her. “I am too agitated; I am going to enter the seminary when I leave here.”

The good woman did not let him leave until she had filled his pockets with provisions. At last Julien set out for the terrible place; from her doorway, the landlady pointed out the way to him.
